To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

cigarette smoking increases the production of the T helper type 2 (Th2)‐associated cytokine IL‐4 by peripheral blood monocytes, and that this increase is related to the number of cigarettes that an individual smokes per day.
cigarette smoking is associated with an increased risk of allergic‐like symptoms, and that this increased risk may be due, at least in part, to an imbalance in IL‐4 and IFN‐γ production.
cigarette smokers produce increased amounts of IL‐4 compared with non‐smokers, and that this effect is more pronounced in heavy smokers than in light smokers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of cigarette smoking on the production of the cytokines, IL‐4 and IFN‐γ, in peripheral blood mononulcear cells of smokers and non‐smokers.
the role of cigarette smoking in the regulation of immune response and its possible role in the development of allergic‐like symptoms.
the effect of cigarette smoking on the immune system.

smoking increases the production of IL‐4 by PBMC.
smoking is a risk factor for asthma and that this is due to the increased IL‐4 production.
cigarette smoking is a risk factor for the development of asthma and that the mechanism of this risk is not fully elucidated.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
smokers have an imbalance in cytokines, favouring IL-4 and this imbalance may be part of a mechanism responsible for increased IgE levels and allergic‐like responses.
smoking increases IL‐4 and decreases IFN‐γ production, which may explain the observed increase in IgE and allergic symptoms.
smoking is an important factor in the development of asthma, and that the mechanisms by which it does this are related to the increased production of IL‐4.

smokers produce more IL‐4 than non‐smokers, which may be responsible for the increases in serum Ig E observed in smokers.
